package_info.package_versions: All private packages created before October 20th (for leak); All packages (for improper authorization flaw)
package_info.why_malicious: The flaws enabled attackers to enumerate private package names (enabling targeted dependency confusion and typosquatting attacks) and to publish new versions of any npm package without proper authorization, potentially allowing malicious code injection into legitimate packages.

required_permissions: read access to public npm replica feed

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Records containing names of private packages (e.g., '@owner/package') published to the public changes feed during maintenance.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Leaked the names of private npm packages to the public replica feed, exposing them to third parties.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Private package names should never be exposed to the public, as this information can be used for targeted attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior is that private package metadata is never published to public feeds; here, private names were exposed.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; private package names should always remain confidential.
key_indicators: Private package names in public change feed

execution_context.file_location: npm registry microservices (authorization and publishing services)
required_permissions: ability to upload a package to npm registry

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Discrepancy between authorization service (validates user for package in URL) and publishing service (publishes based on uploaded package file contents), allowing unauthorized publication.
malicious_snippets.code_language: N/A (logic flaw in service interaction, not a code sample)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Allowed an attacker to publish a new version of any npm package, even if they did not own it, by exploiting mismatched validation between services.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Publishing new versions of packages should be strictly limited to authorized maintainers; this flaw bypassed that control.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior is that only authorized users can publish to a package; here, attackers could publish to any package.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; only maintainers should be able to publish new versions.
key_indicators: Authorization based on URL path, not package file
Mismatch between authorization and publishing targets

attack_chain.action: Attacker enumerates private package names via public replica feed.
attack_chain.leads_to: Knowledge of private package names for targeted attacks.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses leaked names to perform dependency confusion or typosquatting attacks.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victims install malicious packages with similar or identical names.

attack_chain.action: Attacker exploits authorization flaw to publish new versions of legitimate packages without authorization.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is injected into widely used packages, impacting downstream users.

behavioral_signatures: Unusual enumeration of private package names from public feeds
Unauthorized publish events for packages (user not in maintainer list)
Sudden new versions of popular packages from previously unseen accounts
file_indicators: Presence of private package names in public change feeds
Unexpected package version updates without maintainer activity
network_indicators: Automated access to replicate.npmjs.com for package name scraping
Unusual API calls to npm registry for package publishing
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor public npm replica feeds for private package names. Audit publish events to ensure only authorized maintainers are publishing new versions. Flag any publish attempts where the uploader is not listed as a maintainer. Watch for spikes in package installs or new package names similar to private/internal packages (dependency confusion/typosquatting).
